meta.title: Goethe A2 — German
meta.subtitle: 689 words · both directions, as two cards per word
meta.desc: Both study directions in one deck: German → English (see the German, recall the meaning) and English → German (see an English meaning, recall the German). Each direction is a card of its own with its own schedule, so recognising a word and producing it are learnt separately. 689 words for the Goethe-Zertifikat A2, the German qualification awarded by the Goethe-Institut. The vocabulary is the exam board's own published word list, read out of the Wortliste the Goethe-Institut prints for that exam: the 1,157 entries of its alphabetical list and the 246 words of its Wortgruppenliste (the groups it sets apart: the numbers, the days and the times of day, the family, jobs, school subjects, countries and the like). Words the decks of the lower levels already teach are not repeated, which leaves the 689 here. It follows Goethe A1 and comes before Goethe B1, whose list was cut against both. AT THE DEFAULT PACE of ten new cards a day — both directions of a word together, so five words a day — the deck takes 138 days. The cards are ordered roughly by how common the word is in everyday German, so the words you meet most often come first: the order is taken from a frequency list built from film and television subtitles, with a phrase — which a list of single words cannot see — placed by how often it turns up in a corpus of everyday sentences. Every noun carries its article, so the gender is learnt with the word (340 of them), and the article is coloured by gender: der blue, die red, das green. Its plural sits directly beneath it (321 of them). Where a noun names a person its feminine is given too (5), on the exam board's own instruction that beside der Lehrer, die Lehrerin is part of the required vocabulary even though the list does not print it. Each of the 135 verbs carries its full paradigm: the infinitive, the past participle and the auxiliary it takes, then the present, the Präteritum, the Perfekt and the imperative, each in all six persons from ich to sie/Sie. The Perfekt is the point — it is how a German speaker talks about the past, and whether a verb takes haben or sein has to be learnt with the verb. A separable verb is shown as it is really said, ich fahre ab rather than ich abfahre, and the 19 reflexive verbs carry their pronouns (ich freue mich, du freust dich). The polite imperative is given as well as the du and ihr forms: seien Sie ruhig, fahren Sie ab. Adjectives carry their comparative and superlative (96 of them), since German umlauts them unpredictably — groß, größer, am größten. Real example sentences come with 665 of the 689 words, three apiece for 651 of them and one or two for the rest; the sentence corpus has nothing at all for the other 24, which are kept because the word list is set by the exam board and not by the corpus, chosen where possible to show three different inflected forms rather than the same one three times, with the word picked out in colour and a speaker beside it. Word list: Goethe-Zertifikat A2 Wortliste (goethe.de) — the list of words only; the example sentences printed beside them in that document are the Goethe-Institut's own and are not reproduced here. Meanings, genders, plurals, feminines and conjugations: English Wiktionary, via the kaikki.org extraction (CC BY-SA 4.0). Frequency ordering: a word list built from OpenSubtitles (hermitdave/FrequencyWords, CC BY-SA 4.0). Example sentences: Tatoeba (tatoeba.org), CC BY 2.0 FR.
